reasoning: Perold notes the US debt trajectory from $5 trillion in the early 2000s to $40 trillion today, with an annual deficit now at $2 trillion. While he views this as damaging for future generations, from a pure investing perspective he sees it as stimulative and unlikely to reverse. He flags the cognitive dissonance of having to wear two hats — citizen and investor — when assessing macro dynamics.
quote: If you look at the budget deficit, we have $2 trillion and growing. Feels very exponential. The US debt was $5 trillion in early 2000s. It's $40 trillion. It's not all good. A big deficit is very exciting for investing. If the alternative is no deficit, it's not as exciting. The deficit's a problem for the next gen. If you're investing, it's great. That's the conundrum that we're in.

headline: GP-led continuation vehicles are a rich hunting ground for gem businesses at attractive prices, driven by structural DPI pressure forcing sponsors to recycle capital without selling their best assets
reasoning: Perold explains that low DPI is preventing many PE sponsors from raising Fund N+1, pushing them toward continuation vehicles as a way to return cash to existing LPs while retaining their best assets. High Vista has built a dedicated team to underwrite these directly. The lower middle market CVs are especially attractive because entry prices are lower and multiple expansion potential is greater. By definition the assets being put into CVs are the ones sponsors most want to keep, creating a bias toward quality.
quote: In the continuation vehicles, we've hired a team that is now directly looking at continuation vehicles. The beauty there is you can find these gem businesses. If you're a PE sponsor and you have a gem business, there's much more to be done with the business. You can keep rolling up stuff. You can keep adding to it and get a much higher value down the road. Why do you want to sell it? Someone has to take that business and continue to morph it. You're in the best position to do that. Better you keep it and fix it. Yet you want DPI. The continuation vehicle is a way to bring in new investors to take out investors who want out.

headline: Exponential change is real across multiple dimensions simultaneously — AI, GLP-1 healthcare disruption, and runaway US fiscal deficits all compounding at once, creating a uniquely uncertain but alpha-rich environment

Your ability to get an edge is much greater and easier when things are changing rapidly. AI is exponential in what it's doing. On many fronts, it's a tool for productivity that's helping firms get better margins. It's changing our lives, enabling wars. The facets of AI are hard to fathom, and on each dimension, it's exponential. What's happening in healthcare? The exponential change. headline: Short-duration software loans are likely fine despite equity multiple compression driven by terminal value uncertainty — credit investors need EBITDA only through loan maturity, not beyond
reasoning: Perold uses Salesforce as an illustration of how AI disruption is compressing terminal value multiples even for high-growth software companies. However, he argues that credit investors in software are largely insulated because loans are short-dated and only require the company to generate enough cash to repay principal — not to sustain a high terminal value. He believes concern about software private credit is overblown for this reason.
quote: There's a lot of hoopla today, a lot of concern about software and private credit. The software thing is not something we have done. It's out there. It's overblown. We think a lot of the software will be okay because the credit's the short-term loans. They're not long dated. The software you just needed to pay off within a few years and you're going to be okay. It's not like if you own a software firm where if you own the equity, the terminal value of that software firm is critical. Terminal value at a time of disruption is one of the hardest things to sort out.

headline: Micro- and small-cap biotech is a 'beautifully inefficient' market where small specialists can generate outsized returns precisely because large capital is structurally constrained from trading actively
reasoning: Perold identifies micro-cap and small-cap biotech as a structural alpha opportunity because the companies are binary — they either fail and die or succeed and get acquired by large pharma. Large funds are forced into buy-and-hold due to liquidity constraints, while small specialist managers can trade around events and earn excess returns. High Vista backs small, early-stage specialist managers in this space, often spinning out from larger firms, and exits when asset growth compromises their ability to be nimble.
quote: Biotech equities, micro-cap, small-cap biotech stocks. They're all burning money in pursuit of a therapy, or two, or three. They're either going to die if it fails, or if they succeed, they'll get sold to pharma. They'll sell them having revenues. They're burning money, they're diluting shareholders, capital inefficient, risky, and you need to know the signs. You need that specialization. Big money can't come and buy and sell easily. So the big money in biotech is buy and hold. The small money can come in and move around. We have found a way to find partners who are small, extraordinary investors who know the signs and can figure it out. They run small amounts of money. They can put up big numbers, because they can buy and sell while the big guys can't.

headline: Collateralised specialty private credit — GP solutions, data centre construction loans, energy — earns a complexity premium; avoiding commoditised direct lending to sponsors where the edge has been competed away
reasoning: Perold describes High Vista's credit strategy as bespoke, one-loan-at-a-time collateralised lending with specialist originators in each vertical. The firm deliberately avoids direct lending to sponsors because it is commoditised, uncollateralised, and offers insufficient risk-adjusted returns. Current favourites include GP solution financing and data centre construction loans, where hyperscaler credit backstops collateral. Energy credit has become less interesting as the crowd has moved in.
quote: Our credit strategy is always based on where can I find great borrowers where making a loan in size is what they need. Fashion a loan that's highly collateralized that meets our needs takes a lot of work. For that work, we solve their problem, but we get paid an extra return. A return for the work we're putting in, it's a return for complexity. If you can do those well, that's great. We've always avoided direct lending. Lending to sponsors, uncalateralized, where you make a loan and you hope there's enough profits. That's the vast bulk of private credit is direct lending. So we've always avoided that. Because we want to see the collateral. We want to get paid for complexity. It's a far more commodity space in the lending markets.

headline: Venture capital is an essential arrow in any AI strategy — timing is impossible so sustained exposure to great VC firms is the right approach, with a barbell of established brands and newly spun-out stars

headline: Oil at $100/barrel despite escalating Middle East conflict because ~17 million barrels per day still flowing via alternative routes — ship-to-ship transfers, UAE/Oman southern ports, and Saudi west coast — out of a pre-conflict 23 million bpd baseline
reasoning: Hugh Gimbah explains the divergence between alarming geopolitical headlines and a relatively contained oil price by pointing to the volume of crude still moving out of the Middle East through alternative channels. Prior to the conflict, around 23 million barrels per day left the region, predominantly through the Strait of Hormuz. Despite the conflict, approximately 17 million barrels per day can still be accounted for through ship-to-ship transfers, southern UAE and Oman ports, and (until recently) increased flows from Saudi Arabia's west coast. While $100/barrel is not ideal, it is far below what one might expect given the severity of the headlines, and all major parties — including the US, Iran, and China — retain an economic interest in preventing a global recession.
quote: When we now add up all of the different ways the oil is still leaving the Middle East we can explain about 17 million barrels per day of that 23 still getting out. And so the composition has changed because you've had a much greater dependency on some of these alternative ports so again whether that's the south coast of the UAE or the south coast of Oman we're seeing a big pickup in what's known as ship-to-ship transit so this is where local ships are just doing the straights for moves leg and then parking up an alternative port to then connect into those global supply chains... all in all I think this is still the right way to think through this conflict where obviously the politics of the situation is still extremely difficult the headlines are still challenging and let's be clear $100 a barrel oil is not great news for the economy when it's coming through these supply concerns but ultimately I think it's just understanding that there's a lot more oil that's been moving than you would expect if you've just been reading the headlines in the FT.

She argues that high earners often take on proportionally large financial commitments (mortgages, personal loans, car leases, family obligations), meaning income loss is especially devastating. Her five-step preparedness framework centres on: building 6–12 months of emergency cash, auditing discretionary spending, eliminating non-deductible debt, seeking professional financial and accounting advice, and continuous upskilling. She emphasises that redundancy is not a personal failure but a structural workforce shift that will continue, and that having financial breathing room is critical to avoiding panic-driven decisions.
quote: The preparation is really in five steps. And the first one is, um, you know, basically what we want to do is make sure we've got an emergency cash buffer that's really, really important. So that's usually 6 to 12 months worth of your income that's sitting there that you can lean on for the future. The second one is making sure that you understand what all your commitments are, and these are not the regular ones such as mortgage, etc. these are more around the other expenses that we do on a day to day basis, where we might be a little bit more frivolous than most. The third one is making sure that we eliminate any unnecessary non deductible debt. And this is not just the mortgages because we've got to live somewhere. But there's also things personal loans, credit cards you know high leases on cars. Have a look at those and think in the dream of me not having a job, how would I cope with paying for all of these as well?
episode_title: The financial buffer for an AI-driven job loss | the advisory

headline: AI-driven workforce disruption is real but also creates opportunity; redundancy is not personal failure and individuals must build financial flexibility to avoid panic-selling investments
reasoning: Katrina Pulbrook argues that AI is creating both opportunities and disadvantages, particularly around workforce changes and redundancies. She emphasises that a high salary does not equate to wealth if outgoings are equally large, and that individuals must build financial flexibility. In the event of redundancy, people should avoid panic-selling investments or grabbing any available job, and instead treat the situation as a catalyst for reinvention — potentially through consulting, small business, or a career change. The ability to make deliberate choices rather than reactive ones requires prior financial preparation.
quote: What we've got to be aware of though, is that redundancies are not something that's a personal failure. It might feel that way, but it's absolutely not. It's about the changing workforce. But we need to be able to have that flexibility, to be able to use this as a catalyst and know that if you are a got a very big salary coming in the door, that doesn't make you rich, okay. Because of the commitments that you have going out, you have to create your own flexibility. And we also need to be aware that if if you do have a knock on the door and that redundancy package is happening, you've got a vast amount of experience, you have a lot of networks and the ability to be able to use that and also reinvent yourself and make some lifestyle choices and also be able to possibly start, you know, consulting or a small business or going into something completely different. You need to be able to create the choice when that happens, and not just grab any job that comes along because you have a panic and you don't start selling down investments too quickly.

headline: Global economy shifting from an age of efficiency to 'plasticity' — rewiring supply chains, trade, finance and production away from just-in-time specialisation toward resilience, with AI-driven productivity acceleration as the base case
reasoning: Waller argues the global economy is navigating multiple choke points — most recently the closure of the Strait of Hormuz — that are forcing a structural shift from the decades-long model of specialisation and globalisation toward a focus on resilience. He draws an analogy with neuroplasticity: just as the brain rewires itself after disruption, the global economy is rerouting around financial and physical bottlenecks. This 'great rewiring' is expected to play out across trade, finance and production over the next five years. The base case also includes an acceleration of AI diffusion that is expected to drive productivity gains and broader prosperity.
quote: So in a nutshell, we believe that we are moving from an age of efficiency to an age of what we call plasticity. So back in the day at university, next to economics, I also completed a course in cognitive neuroscience. And there I really learned that the brain is able to rewire itself after a disruption. And likewise, the global economy today, which is clearly faced by a lot of choke points, is also working its way around those financial and physical choke points. At the latest physical choke point, of course, being the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. So we are moving from an economy that has been fully being focused on specialization, benefiting from decades of globalization, from an abundance of labor, to a world that is now focusing on resilience instead of being just in time and being over-specialized. And that's basically the great rewiring, which takes place on multiple fronts in trade, in finance and in production.

Historical precedent from post-WWII shows the Fed pinned T-bills at 0.375% and the long bond at 2.5% while inflation peaked at 14.4%, delivering sharply negative real returns to bondholders. The fund expects a repeat of this dynamic — bondholders bearing the cost of fiscal adjustment through financial repression — making nominal yields misleading as a measure of real return.
quote: In the decade post-World War II, the United States pinned T-bills (3 month) at 0.375% and the long bond at 2.5%. The Fed stood ready to buy and absorb any quantity of paper required to pin these yields at levels structurally below growth and runaway inflation which peaked at 14.4% in 1947... Real rates on U.S. debt were held negative in roughly one year in four from 1945 to 1980. In these years, the transfer of value from bondholders to the treasury averaged approximately 3-4% of annual GDP.

headline: USD structural debasement thesis: financial repression and sustained negative real yields are the only politically viable exit from a fiscal debt trap, making the dollar the pressure valve
reasoning: The US has a spending problem compounded by politically entrenched entitlements (social security, federal health, veterans' benefits) and interest payments that already consume 98.4% of annual tax receipts and are growing at a 5.7% CAGR — far exceeding the CBO's 3.9% nominal GDP growth forecast. Austerity is politically impermissible and defaulting on debt would destroy bond markets. The only viable path is financial repression: pinning nominal rates below inflation to erode the real debt burden, as the US did from 1945–1980. Under the current floating dollar regime, the currency must absorb this adjustment. Historical data from the IMF and Reinhart & Rogoff shows roughly 80% of net-debtor countries with debt/GDP above 120% suffered a sovereign default, inflation crisis, or currency crash within a decade. The fund is explicitly building a margin of safety in its global portfolio against USD exposure given this macro setup.
quote: The United States undoubtedly has a spending problem. Ultimately, this problem is compounded by a pernicious permission structure across the American political divide which optimises for short-term sugar hits like unfunded tax cuts, expanded entitlements and one-off transfers as band-aid workarounds to paper over the long-term cracks of the country's significantly deteriorating fiscal outlook... We believe any attempt at true austerity would significantly hurt U.S. equity markets whilst defaulting on debt would have a similar effect on the U.S. bond market. Given the mass citizen wealth tied up in U.S. equities and the widespread perception of U.S. paper as risk-free, we believe both options are, at their core, politically impermissible. This perfect storm affords the U.S. only one real avenue to veer from its disastrous fiscal trajectory. That is financial repression and sustained negative real yields by pinning nominal rates below inflation. Given today's floating U.S. dollar regime, the currency must be the valve to print their way out of this impending crisis.
episode_title: The Silent Threat of US Dollar Exposure

headline: Structurally bearish on the US dollar: applying a 10% per annum currency discount to all US-dollar-denominated earnings to reflect risk of fiscal repression leaking into a weaker exchange rate
reasoning: The fund argues that with US Debt-to-GDP above 120%, PPI inflation at 5.4%, the 10-year yield near 5%, and potential $1.2T in new stimulus (Trump's $5,000 adult dividend proposal), the US fiscal outlook is deteriorating rapidly. Under the current floating-dollar regime (unlike Bretton Woods), the Fed would need to monetise debt by printing dollars, causing structurally higher inflation and a weaker exchange rate. The firm expects a large share of foreign and domestic asset holders to diversify away from US dollars as this dynamic becomes clearer. To manage this risk without direct currency hedging, they apply a 10% per annum translation haircut to future earnings and free cash flow predominantly denominated in USD, and only invest after this adjustment if a stock still offers 75–100% upside over 2–3 years.
quote: To hedge against this risk, we have built a highly conservative margin of safety into our investment process. We apply a 10% per annum currency discount to our view of a business's future earnings power and free cash flow generation whereby the bulk of these earnings are denominated within the United States. To be clear, this haircut is not a view that these businesses will earn 10% less in U.S. dollar terms. Instead, it is a translation adjustment whereby we mark down the base-currency value of these U.S. dollar earnings by 10% per annum to reflect the risk that repression under a floating dollar regime will leak into a structurally weaker exchange rate. Crucially, this 10% is not a forecast. Instead, it is a deliberately conservative margin of safety that we believe is large enough to offer considerable downside protection for our portfolio.

headline: The 52-week high is an irrational anchor: professional investors buy what retail investors sell near that level
reasoning: Andrew Coleman argues that the 52-week high is an arbitrary number with no fundamental significance — it simply measures the highest price over a trailing year with no basis in company value. Despite this, it exerts strong psychological power through anchoring and reference dependence, causing everyday investors to feel uncomfortable and want to sell when a stock approaches that level. He notes that professionals tend to be on the other side of those trades, happily buying what retail sells. He frames this as a classic rational-actor versus human-behaviour split, driven by heuristics and gut feelings rather than rigorous analysis.
quote: The 52 week high is just a number. So why does it hold power over us? It's a great question, right? Because rationally it shouldn't. I mean, if you theoretically believe, as we all, I presume, watching this show do, which is that the good companies over time will rise in price and the poor companies will fall, then simply arbitrarily measuring from one date to another 52 weeks apart and saying the high within that period means anything, of course, is irrational. It means absolutely nothing. But I think it's a fascinating thing about how we as humans interact... the rational actor does things mathematically and does them rationally and considered and researched and rigorous. And then the humans do things with heuristics, rules of thumb. We get gut feelings. And I think the 52 week high ends up playing on a few of those, but in particular, the concept of anchoring.
episode_title: Wealthy & Wise | the most dangerous number in investing

headline: Disposition effect drives retail selling at highs: investors lock in gains without knowing fundamental value, using price paid as their only reference point
reasoning: Andrew Grant explains that the disposition effect — the tendency to sell winners and hold losers — is the primary driver of retail selling near 52-week highs. Investors anchor to their purchase price; when the current price exceeds it, the impulse is to lock in the gain. The flip side is 'get-even-itis', where investors hold losing positions waiting to recover to break-even. He emphasises that retail investors lack the valuation tools to judge whether a price is fundamentally cheap or expensive, so they rely on the 52-week range as a crude barometer, using it as a sell signal without any fundamental basis.
quote: One of the most common ways in which people make decisions is I bought the stock at a price, and now it's currently worth more than what I paid for it. So this is something called the disposition effect. It means I want to sell the stock because I'm going to lock in this game, right? So making a profit, that seems to be what we're all aiming for in the stock price... what we don't know when it comes to trading stocks and what individual investors aren't really good at is understanding how much should the stock be worth, right? The stock could be worth $32 on the stock market. I'm like, is that a good price? Is that a bad price? I don't know, right. All I can say is it's worth more than what I paid for. And I can see relative to where the stock's been over the past year here. It's at a high price time to sell. So that's the logic. It's like the barometer the temperature. The temperature is higher than where it's been. Now it's time to sell.
episode_title: Wealthy & Wise | the most dangerous number in investing

headline: Focusing on dividend income and whole-portfolio thinking reduces purchase-price anchoring and improves long-term decision-making
reasoning: Andrew Grant argues that investors can counter purchase-price anchoring by shifting focus to two things: the ongoing dividend income generated by holdings (which reduces the urge to sell quickly), and the portfolio-level rationale for each position rather than treating each stock as a standalone P&L. He notes that viewing stocks in isolation causes investors to underestimate the diversification and risk-offsetting value each holding provides, leading to sub-optimal sell decisions driven by arbitrary price levels.
quote: I think to add to his point, you know, there are other things we can think about that aren't related to the purchase price. We can think about if I'm buying stocks, perhaps focus on the dividends that you're getting from the stocks and hold that as part of the rationale for buying the stock and holding the stock. So you're not likely to want to sell out quickly if the stock is generating some profits for you on a, you know, on an annual or semi-annual basis. That's that's one way of sort of getting the purchase price out of your mind. And secondly, I think, right. Well, what did I buy the stock for in the first place? Is it to make a quick profit or is it to, you know, generate a portfolio for the long run? And I think the other side of this is when we focus on separating out our assets like stock A, stock B stock, see as if to say their individual investments. And don't think of our whole portfolio, then we're ignoring why we might want to hold different pieces of the pie, because some of them will allow us to diversify our risk or offset other risks that we might be holding.

headline: Anchoring bias around 52-week highs causes investors to sell winners and hold losers — use intrinsic value or PE-based anchors instead of purchase price
reasoning: Andrew Coleman explains that anchoring on arbitrary reference points like the 52-week high or the price paid leads to the classic mistake of cutting flowers and watering weeds — selling strong performers and holding weak ones. He argues the antidote is to anchor on intrinsic value: if the asset is worth $50 and the market offers $80, sell; if it offers $35, hold. For investors who cannot estimate intrinsic value, he recommends anchoring on the PE ratio or earnings yield rather than the nominal share price, so that rising earnings do not trigger a false sell signal.
quote: Number one, if you're capable and all our team members are, we have a piece of software that helps us do this, or you may have access to the data, get a good understanding of the intrinsic value of the asset, because that's really what matters if the asset is worth $50. If Mr. Market offers you 80. Take it. If he offers you 35. Don't take it, even if that's the highest price it's been for the last year. I mean, that's common sense. If you can't do that, though, or that's just a lot of work and you don't want to do it so you're capable, but you are at the stage of life where that doesn't seem like fun. Then anchor. If you're going to anchor on anything, anchor on something like the PE ratio rather than the price you paid. Because that way, if the company's earnings rise, at least you're not penalizing yourself on an arbitrary share price.
episode_title: Wealthy & Wise | the most dangerous number in investing

reasoning: Andrew Coleman argues that the 52-week high in isolation is the 'most dangerous number in investing' because it causes investors to turn off their brains and make reflexive decisions. headline: Anchoring bias driven by evolutionary scarcity psychology; trading platforms amplify it by always showing the purchase price rather than intrinsic value
reasoning: Andrew Coleman argues that humans evolved in conditions of scarcity, creating a psychological drive to lock in gains and avoid losses — the same impulse that causes overeating. In the stock market, this manifests as anchoring on the purchase price rather than intrinsic or relative value. Trading software reinforces this by displaying the price paid every time an investor logs in. Brokerages benefit from this bias because it encourages more trading, generating commission revenue regardless of portfolio outcomes. The rational alternative is to anchor on intrinsic value or a relevant valuation ratio such as P/E, not the nominal price paid.
quote: The point you should be anchored on if you were perfectly rational is not the price you paid, but what is the stock worth now? From an intrinsic value point of view? Or alternatively, if you don't want to put that amount of work into work out intrinsic value, at least anchor not on the price, but on the relevant ratio. So on the relevant p e ratio. You know, I bought company A on a p e ratio of 15. The fact that the share price is higher but the p e ratio is now 12 says it's the wrong time to sell. If anything, I'm giving up value just for the sake of trading. But we don't do that, and brokerages have an encouragement to us not to do that. The more they can give us information that anchors us on the price we paid, the more likely we are to trade. And of course, they make money off the trade, not on the stock of our wealth.

headline: Individual investors consistently mistimed — buying after runs and replacing sold stocks with ones that go up even more; doing the opposite of the crowd may offer an edge
reasoning: Andrew Grant notes that individual investors lack the full information set and analytical capability of professional investors, leaving them working with limited data. Behavioural finance research shows retail investors are poor at timing: they tend to buy stocks that have already risen too much, and when they sell, they replace those positions with stocks that subsequently appreciate even further. This implies a contrarian signal — buying what individuals want to sell and selling what they want to buy may generate excess returns. The utility derived from selling at a profit also reinforces the disposition effect, making investors reluctant to sell at a loss even when it would be rational.
quote: Research in behavioral finance shows that individuals aren't good at timing their decisions. Right. So in other words, they'll buy stocks after they've gone up too much. And then they'll replace stocks in their portfolio with stocks then end up going up even more. So it ends up that if you followed what the individual does and do the exact opposite, so you buy the stocks they want to sell and you sell the stocks they want to buy, there's probably some likelihood of earning a profit.

She says the driver is not inflation expectations but real yields, which are rising because of massive demand for capital including AI infrastructure build-out and elevated fiscal spending. She also points out that the transmission mechanism from long-end rates to the real economy has weakened because corporates and households locked in very low rates post-COVID, especially via 30-year mortgages, leaving both consumer and corporate balance sheets relatively healthy.
quote: Where am I paying a little more attention? I would say is the long end of the curve, right? My view again is the past couple of decades have been a bit the aberration here. Actually, if you look at the 70s, the 80s and 90s, we were happily in a world above 5% on the 10 year for quite some time there. And again, that's a function of huge demand for capital, huge AI infrastructure build out here. And I will be honest, fiscal spending being higher than it should be. And so demand and supply at that end of the curve. headline: Russia/Tinkov investment: right on the company fundamentals, wrong on country tail risk — Russia discount was warranted; lesson is to stress-test extreme scenarios including 5% probability events that can permanently impair capital
reasoning: Iona held Tinkov, a high-quality Russian digital bank serving underbanked consumers, which was performing extremely well operationally and was attractively valued given the Russia discount. When Russia invaded Ukraine all of that became irrelevant and the position was a total loss. The lesson was that being right on the company is insufficient if you are not humble enough about country-level tail risk and black swan scenarios. She now insists on stress-testing both bull and bear cases from first principles, including low-probability events that could permanently impair 100% of capital.
quote: So in Russia, it was an emerging market bank basically and it was an extraordinary business. Frankly, one of the best digital banks I had seen and amazing customer proposition, amazing, NPS scores to kind of just solving. It was a digital bank in Russia. So it started off actually as kind of credit cards and debit cards for the lower and less affluent population... When Russia invaded Ukraine, I learned you can be completely right about the company but still have a disastrous investment because you were insufficiently humble about the country and the tail risk as well. So the lesson for me was just to be very creative in both the bull and the bear case and really stress test the numbers and not just put through a bear case in these scenarios that we've seen historically... you have to put in a bull case. If you had just put in a bull case from the past 10 years, you would have completely missed this trade. So I think you've got to think outside the box from first principles about what the real risks are and even the 5% probability outcome that could permanently impair 100% of your capital.

headline: Broad put options preferred over gold, credit or unlisted assets as the equity hedge replacement — convex, liquid in a crisis, and allow holding more equities for the same portfolio risk
reasoning: Sherwood favours broad put options to replace bonds as portfolio diversifiers in balanced, diversified real-return and global equity allocation funds. He cites four reasons: options become convex when equity markets are stressed; downside risk is known upfront (the premium paid); put options are highly liquid in a sell-off allowing quick monetisation when volatility peaks; and they allow the portfolio to hold more equities over the cycle for the same level of risk, which is positive for long-run returns. He contrasts this favourably with gold, credit and unlisted assets, which lack liquidity and convexity in a crisis.
quote: I think a much better alternative is the use of broad options and we use those fairly judiciously in our balanced funds, our diversified real return fund and of course our 100% equities global allocation alpha fund. And we use them in all of our funds for four reasons. Firstly, because options do become convex when equity markets are stressed. Secondly and importantly, you actually know your downside risk with an option, which is just simply the price of putting it on. Thirdly, put options are highly liquid in a sell-off. And that's important because the protection you've enjoyed can be monetized quickly when volatility or equities really are oversold. And with options you can hold more equities over the cycle for the same level of portfolio risk. So you put all that together, it's good for returns.

headline: Selective RMBS investing with rigorous deal-by-deal stress testing; rejecting roughly 40% of deals keeps portfolio arrears at 2.59% versus 3.5% for the broader market
reasoning: The investment process involves a three-step loan-level analysis: forecasting arrears and foreclosure rates on every individual mortgage, running foreclosures through each deal's cash flow structure to ensure full repayment of every tranche, and applying a binary approval gate where any forecast of capital loss prohibits investment. Approximately one-third of deals reviewed are rejected, with four in ten failing due to forecast cash flow losses. This disciplined selection has produced portfolio arrears of 2.59% versus 3.5% for the broader RMBS market and zero losses across historical stress episodes. The speaker presents this as a reflection of process quality rather than a shortage of supply, as rejected deals remain available for purchase.
quote: Every deal is stress tested before you can buy it. It's a three-step process. First, we analyze the pool loan by loan, forecasting arrears and foreclosure rates on every individual mortgage. Second, we run those foreclosures through the deal's cash flow structure to test that every layer of the capital stack is repaid in full over the life of the deal. And third, it's a binary decision. If the model forecasts a capital loss, the deal isn't approved, and portfolio managers are prohibited from investing in that particular deal... We only approve about 2/3 of what we look at. So, four in 10 deals fail because of the forecast on cash flow loss. Those rejected deals are available to buy. This is a reflection process, not a shortage of supply. We just don't invest in everything. And you can see the outcome in our numbers. Our arrears numbers are 2.59% sitting against 3.5% for the broader market.
